transcript.text: hotpoint SA2 oven not heatin on fan, grill ok. wat does SA2 mean??

SA2 isn't an error code. On Hotpoint it's normally the start of the model or series name, typically their built-in electric single ovens. The full model number usually has more letters and numbers after it, printed on the rating plate around the door frame. You don't need it for now. The grill working is a useful clue. It means power is reaching the oven and the controls are at least partly working, so the fault is probably in the part of the circuit that only the fan setting uses. In rough order of likelihood: 1. The fan oven element. This is the round element hidden behind the back panel, around the fan, and it's the most common cause of exactly this symptom.
2. A burnt connector or wire at that element.
3. The function selector switch or the oven thermostat not switching that element on. It's also worth ruling out a simple setting slip first. Quick checks, with the oven cool: 1. Check the setting. Make sure the knob is on the fan heating symbol (a fan with a ring around it), not defrost, which is a fan with no ring and runs the fan with no heat. Also make sure the temperature knob is turned up, say to 180°C, and that the temperature light comes on. If it was on defrost, that's your answer.
2. Look through the glass at the back of the oven to see if the fan is spinning. If it spins but the oven stays cold, the fan motor is fine and the heating side is the problem. If the fan isn't turning, the fan motor becomes a suspect instead.
3. Try another oven setting, such as conventional top and bottom heat, if yours has it. If that heats but fan mode doesn't, it points strongly towards the fan element or its wiring. If no oven setting heats (only the grill), the thermostat or selector switch becomes more likely. Let me know what you find on those, especially the fan and the other settings, and I'll narrow it down.
ok checked. fan at the back isnt turning, just a low hum from it. top+bottom heat does work but slowly. SA2 is printed on the trim above the door, display just shows the time

That changes the picture. A fan that hums but won't turn means power is reaching the fan motor, but the motor can't spin. That points away from the element and towards the fan itself. In fan mode the oven relies on that fan to move heat from the ring element around the cavity. With it stalled, the oven will heat poorly or not at all, and some ovens cut the element out to protect it. Top and bottom heat doesn't use the fan, which is why it still works. 1. A seized or worn fan motor. A dry or worn bearing is the classic hum-but-no-spin fault.
2. Something fouling the fan blade, such as a blade knocked out of shape or a loose rear cover catching it. 1. Make it safe. 2. Look through the slots in the back panel for anything caught on the blade, and check the back panel is firmly fixed and not bent inwards.
3. Gently nudge the fan blade through the slots with something non-metallic, like the handle of a wooden spoon. - Stiff, gritty or won't move: the motor bearing has seized, and the fan motor is the likely part.
• Spins freely and there's nothing catching: the motor itself is probably failing and can't start under power. It's still most likely the fan motor, though a wiring fault to it is possible.
• Catching on the cover or something stuck: free it or refit the cover, then try fan mode again. Until it's sorted, avoid the fan settings. A stalled, humming motor can overheat. Top and bottom heat is fine to use meanwhile, just allow extra time. It may be slow simply because it's working without the fan, though if it's very slow the element could be weak as well. Checking an oven fan motor is a common repair. It usually means taking off the back panel and fitting from behind, so a confident DIYer can sometimes do it, but an engineer is the safer choice if you're not sure. When you get to buying a part, you'll need the full model number. That's on the rating plate on the door frame edge, not the SA2 on the trim. Once the fan runs, check that fan mode actually heats too, in case the element has also suffered.
isolated it at the cooker switch first, then tried the blade by hand. its very stiff and feels gritty. also got a slight hot smell from the back once, not now tho

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. That settles the main question. A blade that is very stiff and gritty by hand, plus a hum with no spin under power, is a common sign of a seized fan motor bearing. I'm fairly confident the cavity fan motor is the likely faulty part. A motor in good order should spin freely and smoothly with a light flick. A stalled motor that keeps getting power can overheat its windings, and that may be all the smell was. It could also have scorched the wiring or connectors to it, or another connection at the back, and you can't see those without taking it apart. Please don't use the oven at all now, top and bottom heat included, until a qualified engineer has checked it. Keep it isolated at the cooker switch. That means it's off and isolated while you wait, as you already have it. 1. Remove the back panel and fan motor and confirm the bearing is rough. That's what suggests the motor as the failed part.
2. Inspect the motor wiring, the fan element connectors and the main terminal connection for any heat damage linked to the smell.
3. Once a new motor is fitted, run fan mode at about 180°C to confirm it heats properly. The element has been working without airflow, so this checks it hasn't suffered too. Fan motor swaps are a routine, usually moderate-cost repair on a built-in oven, so it's normally well worth fixing rather than replacing. The engineer will need the full model number from the rating plate on the door frame edge to get the right motor.
